questions.q: A team needs to run Hive and Presto side by side on the same long-lived cluster, with custom instance types for one specific nightly job. Which tool fits, and why?
options: EMR — it allows fine-grained cluster tuning, specific instance types, and multiple open-source tools co-located on the same cluster
Glue — its serverless model is designed for exactly this kind of multi-tool, long-lived cluster
Databricks — it is AWS-native and integrates directly with EMR clusters
None of the three support running Hive and Presto together
questions.explain: This is precisely the kind of requirement that needs EMR's cluster-level control — Glue's managed environment doesn't expose that level of tuning or let you co-locate arbitrary open-source tools.

questions.q: What does Glue optimize for compared to EMR?
options: Managed simplicity — no cluster to size or patch, billed per job run — at the cost of fine-grained cluster control
Maximum control over instance types and cluster configuration
Being a multi-cloud platform
Running Hive and Presto together on shared infrastructure
questions.explain: Glue trades cluster-level control for operational simplicity — you don't manage the underlying compute, but you also can't tune it beyond what Glue exposes.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why do some teams choose Databricks over Glue or EMR?
options: For its notebook-first collaborative developer experience, Delta Lake, and multi-cloud portability — not because Glue or EMR are technically incapable
Because Databricks is a native AWS service with no additional cost
Because it's the only platform that supports Spark
Because Glue and EMR cannot process data larger than 1 GB
questions.explain: The lesson frames Databricks as a legitimate but different choice — teams pay for the collaborative notebook experience and cross-cloud portability, not because the AWS-native options are broken.

questions.q: What operational responsibility shifts to the team when choosing EMR over Glue?
options: Cluster sizing and patching cadence become the team's responsibility instead of being fully managed
IAM permissions become unnecessary
S3 integration must be built entirely from scratch
Spark itself must be written in a different language
questions.explain: EMR gives you the cluster to control, which also means you (or your team) take on sizing and patching decisions Glue's serverless model handles for you.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects this lesson's overall framing of EMR vs. Glue vs. Databricks?
options: Each optimizes for something different (simplicity, control, or developer experience) — there is no universally "best" choice
EMR is objectively obsolete and should never be used
Glue should always be chosen over the other two
Databricks is an AWS service and therefore always the safest default
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly avoids recommending one tool as universally best, instead giving a framework based on what each option optimizes for.
